items.content:
RT @joshua_saxe: Thoughts on php2shell and the overall looming crisis in cybersecurity

If you'd been appropriately pricing in that we'd see this and many more celebrity zero-days at an increasing rate, this is a positive update; defenders found this issue, alongside tens of thousands of others in the last year, before widespread exploitation, and it's being patched.

Real attackers will exploit this, but we shouldn't expect a recognizable blip in overall cyber damages in the next couple quarters, because easier initial access to victim networks wasn't a core bottleneck for attackers, and because defenders are better positioned to adopt AI automation than attackers, and are doing so faster; this advantage will persist through at least H1 2027, and possibly longer, IMO.

Why I think this: consider that, in general and on average, defenders have access to default-world capital networks and AI talent, often as a function of how central they are to Internet and societal infrastructure.  They have consistent, reliable access to AI inference from open- and closed-weight providers.

Criminal attackers, on the other hand, face the threat of arrest, difficulty accessing AI talent, and unreliable access to AI inference.  They're competing for and attempting to retain talent willing to risk arrest and sanctions, and willing to live a life of crime.

Nation-state attackers, meanwhile, operate within military and intelligence bureaucracies that have historically lagged private industry in adopting technologies, from mobile devices to drones.  Non-US-aligned nation-state attackers also face challenges in reliably, consistently, and secretly accessing US frontier models.

So, all in all, AI is making offensive capabilities cheaper, but that doesn't immediately translate into damages.  At this point, this is a robust finding from the entire 2022–26 period; as in the rest of the economy, we haven't seen a big AI-driven productivity bump among attackers, and attackers are even more disadvantaged than your average business or civilian state agency.

Of course, this won't last forever!  How do we exploit our current, limited defense-dominant window?  Getting to a good-enough steady state will require creative thinking.  I liked @chrisrohlf's piece on eliminating attack surface in OSS applications because it identifies leverage points for eliminating whole classes of risk using 2026-era AI (https://t.co/L2alFLbNs9).

We also need to revisit formal verification, control flow integrity, dynamic taint tracking, and the like, now that AI can make them more practical than they used to be.  We also have an enormous overhang of underdeployed defensive technology.  Honeypots, honeytokens, sandboxing, multi-factor authentication, and application allowlisting are all less widely deployed than they should be because businesses calculated they weren't worth it.

The AI industry should recognize that heavily gated trusted access programs have failed as a strategy; php2shell was identified by defenders first, and we need more defenders identifying more bugs faster.  The defense-dominant window is exactly the moment to pour gas on the fire of diffusion of as-cheap-as-possible AI security capabilities that disproportionately advantage defenders.

If you don't like what this means for attacker access to models, I agree with you!  The answer is to solve the quadratic coordination problem among cyber organizations, AI companies, governments, and Internet infrastructure providers by building institutions that identify attacker groups, kick them off inference platforms, and, wherever possible, get them arrested.  This is an operational threat intelligence / threat interdiction problem, not a trusted access program problem.

This is actually the part that worries me even more.

Some interesting reports from the last few days:

01) ARTEX / ConnectWise

Microsoft reports that Storm-0940 used ARTEX in a large-scale campaign targeting more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants. Up to 2,900 authentication attempts per minute, with privileged cloud access achieved in under three hours in some cases.

CrowdStrike found evidence of AI-driven attacks against South Korean financial organizations, including exposed Claude Code sessions and ARTEX configurations. DeepSeek, GLM and Grok were used in the attacker's setup.

https://t.co/kOiEqSEwUi

03) Cairn / 100+ Compromised Companies

NorForge investigated exposed Cairn instances used for autonomous hacking campaigns. More than 1,100 attack projects in one cluster alone. Reuters identified over 100 companies whose websites had been compromised.

Estimated AI costs: around $5 per task, according to NorForge. That's ridiculously cheap.

https://t.co/54Ir7IeY4Q

04) Four More Agentic AI Campaigns

CrowdStrike documented four additional threat actors using AI agents for real intrusion campaigns, including attacks against healthcare organizations and government entities.

https://t.co/rte8LIYL90

What concerns me is how quickly the economics of offensive operations are changing.

Finding vulnerabilities, testing attack paths, adapting payloads, trying something else when an exploit fails, and eventually deploying a webshell. Much of this can now be delegated to agents that keep working for hours.

And with open-weight models and freely available agent harnesses, the cost of running these operations is dropping significantly.

We've been talking about AI changing offensive security for quite a while. These reports show that it's already happening in real-world intrusions.

And I'm pretty sure we're only seeing a fraction of it.

I took this opportunity to revisit and update my 2022 presentation on post-exploitation detection.

The exploit may be new, or completely different from anything we’ve seen before, but the activity that follows often fits patterns we already understand. Generic detection rules can recognize those patterns without knowing which vulnerability was used. A rule written for one incident can therefore help detect another, years later.

That’s the idea I’ve been talking about for years, and what the presentation explains in practical terms. The slides walk through how to turn an observation into a useful rule, which data you need, and why a match still needs context.

I'm excited for the opportunities to liberate closed hardware this provides. We know hardware, particularly abandoned IoT devices are unlikely to be updating their revocation lists and root CAs. I'm not sure how well the revocations work in that world given the difference in the CA trust model in use there.

items.content:
RT @HackingLZ: LLMs...Letting me do fun things I never would have wasted time on. 

 "I reviewed all 30 public GitHub repos for PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619) by reading code only. The slide has the full
  grouped table; the headline findings:

 Nothing works against a real target. Every genuine memory-corruption chain is lab-bound: it needs exact per-build offsets, display_errors=On, a single prefork mod_php worker, and a specific image.
  Independent reviewers (allureluoli, dinosn, Gi1gamesh123) and the leaked primary source itself all converge on "no public artifact achieves code execution" on the patched core bug. Every real shell
  in these repos comes from an app-side LFI or deserialization sink, not the CVE.

  Three are original and real, all lab-only. 9bie (the source of the Set-Cookie leak chain), Marven11 (the most sophisticated, a true in-band leak), and Karasawa2025 (whose "Fermat" troll description
  hides a working ROP + display_errors=off exploit). These are the only ones with a genuine ASLR-defeating leak primitive that is their own.

  Most are copies. One original (9bie) spawned five derivatives:
  - twili8 is an outright uncredited rip-off: its own README still says git clone 9bie/... and the Docker files are byte-identical.
  - godylockz and xuehuolll are byte-identical to each other.
  - dinosn and 3em0 are credited ports that add value.

  Three are mislabeled. iQingshan, KarimUD7 (≈98% the same code), and Gi1gamesh123 exploit a different bug entirely (the Calif unserialize var_hash UAF) against their own planted endpoints, filed
  under the php2shell CVE numbers.

  The rest is noise. The most-starred repo (ikow, 905★) delivers the least: broken or stubbed chains with the two "real" ones paywalled behind Substack. eness (558★) is a leakless forge that can't
  defeat ASLR. syrex1013 ships AI-generated fake CVEs in a side directory. Whackermelon hallucinates a non-existent openai/php2shell-checker. lcfr-eth is a parody with a memecoin address, and Icex0
  is an empty repo. The genuinely honest work is the crash labs (allureluoli, slabbdev, 0x4148), which prove the bug without claiming RCE.

  The ASLR column, star counts, copy lineage, and the specific "tell" for each repo are all in the table. The page is private to your account; use the Share menu if you want to send it to the team"

items.content:
In 2008, Debian disclosed that a change intended to silence Valgrind warnings had broken OpenSSL's random number generator.

The change removed code that mixed entropy into its internal state, leaving the process ID as the only meaningful source of variability. Attackers could precompute the possible keys instead of breaking the cryptography.

In 2026, eight of eMudhra's intermediate CA private keys turned out to be:

4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237.
